result.paraphrase:
Software testing faces the fundamental problem of statistically sound extrapolation from program behaviors observed during testing. For example, after running a fuzzer for a week, a security researcher still has no way to estimate (1) the total number of feasible program branches when only a fraction has been covered, (2) the extra time needed to cover 10% more branches or, equivalently, the coverage that would be reached in another day, or (3) the remaining risk that a vulnerability exists despite none being found. Not finding a vulnerability does not prove that none exists, even if the fuzzer runs for a week or a year. Thus, testing offers no formal guarantee of correctness.

In this article, I reveal an unexpected link to the seemingly unrelated field of ecology and present a statistical framework that treats Software Testing and Analysis as Discovery of Species (STADS). To study arthropod diversity in a tropical rain forest, ecologists first sample many individuals, identify their species, and extrapolate from the sample to the forest as a whole. In ecology, estimating (1) the total number of species, (2) the extra sampling effort needed to find 10% more species, or (3) the chance of discovering a new species are classic problems. STADS applies more than three decades of ecological biostatistics research to the core extrapolation problem in automated test generation. Our preliminary empirical study shows strong estimator performance even for AFL, a state-of-the-art vulnerability detection tool with adaptive sampling bias. The STADS framework delivers statistical correctness guarantees with quantifiable accuracy.
